did_you_know.text: Ecclesiastes presents the righteous, the wise, and their deeds as being in the “hand of God,” but emphasizes that no one knows in advance whether love or hatred awaits them.
The chapter emphasizes that the same fate may overtake different people: the righteous and the wicked, the clean and the unclean, and both those who offer sacrifices and those who do not.
The saying “A living dog is better than a dead lion” expresses a preference for life over death: even a humble life is better than great status lost through death.
According to Ecclesiastes, the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing; this highlights the difference between the awareness of the living and the inactivity that follows death.
After describing uncertainty and death, Ecclesiastes turns to the living and encourages them to eat joyfully and drink with a glad heart.
Ecclesiastes presents married life and love as a person’s portion during life and in their “toil” under the sun, encouraging people to enjoy them while life lasts.
The verse “Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with all your strength” emphasizes the importance of acting in the present, because in Sheol there is no work, planning, knowledge, or wisdom.

The chapter teaches that no personal advantage guarantees success: speed does not guarantee victory, strength does not guarantee victory in battle, and wisdom and knowledge do not guarantee wealth or favor.
People do not know when disaster will overtake them; Ecclesiastes compares human beings to fish and birds that are suddenly caught in a net or a snare.

In the story of the small city, a poor but wise man saves the city through his wisdom, but afterward no one remembers him. From this, Ecclesiastes concludes that wisdom is better than strength and weapons of war, even though its value is sometimes not recognized.
